name: Rent split
seoTitle: Rent split Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Rent split: work out share of the rent ([hidden]) from the total rent and the floor space – Bedrooom 1. A free finance calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the total rent, the floor space – Bedrooom 1 and number of people and the Rent split calculator solves for share of the rent ([hidden]). It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Rent split calculator work?
sections.html:
The Rent split calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports share of the rent ([hidden]) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (number of bedrooms); then you type in the total rent, the floor space – Bedrooom 1, number of people (Bedroom 1) and number of people (Bedroom 2).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

  • Pick the option that matches your case — 3 options, such as one, two and three. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in person(s).
  • A number, expressed in person(s).

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Rent split calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Share of the rent=(floor space – Bedrooom 1 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3))
Each person in this room pays=((floor space – Bedrooom 1 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3)) ÷ number of people)
Share of the rent=(floor space – Bedrooom 2 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3))
Each person in this room pays=((floor space – Bedrooom 2 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3)) ÷ number of people)
Share of the rent=(floor space – Bedrooom 3 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3))
Each person in this room pays=((floor space – Bedrooom 3 × total rent ÷ (floor space – Bedrooom 1 + floor space – Bedrooom 2 + floor space – Bedrooom 3)) ÷ number of people)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Total rent = 10, Number of bedrooms set to One, Floor space – Bedrooom 1 = 10 m² and Floor space – Bedrooom = 10 m². Working through the relationship above gives Total area = 30 ft², Share of the rent = 3 and Each person in this room pays = 3.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Total area = 30 ft², Share of the rent = 3 and Each person in this room pays = 3 should be roughly the size you expected from Total rent = 10 and Number of bedrooms set to One.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Rent split calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total rent, the floor space – Bedrooom 1 and number of people — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Rent split calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns share of the rent ([hidden]), derived from the total rent, the floor space – Bedrooom 1 and number of people. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Rent split calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total rent, the floor space – Bedrooom 1 and number of people, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total rent in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total rent opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total area = 30 ft². Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Rent split calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
